extracted.subtask_description: Rules, equivalences, and translation techniques for first-order quantifiers, bounded quantifiers, and related set-notation used in introductory quantificational logic and elementary set theory. Includes negation laws, ordering effects, distribution facts, uniqueness, and set-family unions/intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of quantifiers matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing the order of quantifiers can change the meaning of a formula (e.g., ∀x∃y(x+y=5) is true but ∃y∀x(x+y=5) is false).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret ∀x∃y as 'for each x there exists (possibly different) a y' and ∃y∀x as 'there is a single y that works for every x.' Examples: x+y=5 and 'everyone likes someone' vs 'there is someone who everyone likes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading quantifier pairs of the same type as unordered
rubrics_metrics.description: Two quantifiers of the same type (both ∀ or both ∃) can always be switched without changing meaning (e.g., ∀x∀y and ∀y∀x are equivalent; ∃x∃y and ∃y∃x are equivalent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read ∃x∃y or ∀x∀y as 'there are objects x and y such that...' Use this when translating sentences like 'Someone has a teacher who is younger than he is' vs 'There is a teacher of someone who is older than the teacher.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier negation laws (unbounded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation interacts with quantifiers via: ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x) and ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these laws to move negation past quantifiers and to reexpress negative statements positively. Examples show stepwise rewriting using conditional and DeMorgan's laws to produce equivalent positive forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier negation laws (bounded quantifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The negation laws extend to bounded quantifiers: ¬∃x∈A P(x) ≡ ∀x∈A ¬P(x) and ¬∀x∈A P(x) ≡ ∃x∈A ¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive these by expanding bounded quantifiers as abbreviations (e.g., ∃x∈A P ≡ ∃x(x∈A∧P)). Example: show ¬∀x∈A P(x) ≡ ∃x∈A ¬P(x) through expansion and previous negation laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: negate then reexpress positively using logical equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: To negate quantified statements and obtain an equivalent positive statement, apply quantifier negation laws, DeMorgan's laws, and conditional equivalences in sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples: Negating 'Everyone has a relative he doesn't like' and producing an equivalent positive form 'There is someone who likes all his relatives.' Step-by-step symbolic manipulations are shown and recommended as a method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal quantifier distributes over conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: ∀x(P(x) ∧ Q(x)) is equivalent to (∀x P(x)) ∧ (∀x Q(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Everyone is bright-eyed and bushy-tailed' (∀x(E(x)∧T(x))) is equivalent to 'Everyone is bright-eyed and everyone is bushy-tailed' (∀xE(x) ∧ ∀xT(x)). Use this distributivity in proofs (e.g., to show set equality by proving two subset inclusions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential quantifier does NOT distribute over conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: In general ∃x(P(x) ∧ Q(x)) is not equivalent to (∃x P(x)) ∧ (∃x Q(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'There is someone who is both bright-eyed and bushy-tailed' versus 'There is someone bright-eyed and there is someone bushy-tailed' — the latter allows different individuals. Be careful when manipulating ∃ with conjunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential quantifier distributes over disjunction (exercise/claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: ∃x(P(x) ∨ Q(x)) is equivalent to (∃x P(x)) ∨ (∃x Q(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text poses this as an exercise to show; treat it as a standard equivalence to be used when appropriate (contrast with failure of ∃ over ∧).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique-existence abbreviation (∃!x) and formal expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: The notation ∃!x P(x) abbreviates 'there is exactly one x such that P(x),' and can be expanded as ∃x(P(x) ∧ ¬∃y(P(y) ∧ y≠x)) (or equivalent formulations using ∀ to enforce uniqueness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used frequently; gives a succinct replacement for longer formulas expressing uniqueness. Example: 'John likes exactly one person' can be written ∃!x L(j,x) and expanded accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free vs bound variables / recognizing free variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing statements, identify which variables are free (not bound by quantifiers) and how that affects the formula's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask to find free variables in formulas (e.g., formulas with parameter w). Pay attention when translating English statements into symbolic form to mark which variables are intended as quantified vs free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded quantifier shorthand and expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Notation ∀x∈A P(x) abbreviates ∀x(x∈A → P(x)); ∃x∈A P(x) abbreviates ∃x(x∈A ∧ P(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for restricting quantification to subsets (e.g., ∀x∈R+ ∃y∈R-(y^2=x)). Bounded forms can always be expanded into unbounded quantifiers with conjunction/implication as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacuous truth consequences (empty domain effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = ∅ then ∃x∈A P(x) is false for any P, while ∀x∈A P(x) is true for any P (vacuously true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications: the empty set is a subset of every set; statements like 'All unicorns are purple' are vacuously true. Use quantifier negation laws to justify these facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outermost-symbol rule for expanding notation
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating complex mathematical notation to logical form, begin with the outermost symbol and expand its definition first (e.g., decide whether to expand power set, intersection, or subset first depending on outer structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show different choices yield different ease of expansion; use the 'outermost-first' rule to guide decomposition of expressions like x∈P(A∩B) vs x∈P(A)∩P(B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing distinctness when required
rubrics_metrics.description: When a natural-language sentence requires distinct objects, explicitly include inequality (e.g., to express 'at least two different people' use ∃y∃z(y≠z ∧ ...)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'everyone likes at least two people' must include y ≠ z; 'x is a bigamist' requires ∃y∃z(M(x,y) ∧ M(x,z) ∧ y≠z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conditional and DeMorgan laws in quantifier manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformations often rely on rewriting implications as disjunctions and applying DeMorgan's laws before moving negations across quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked derivations show steps like (P→Q) equivalent to (¬P ∨ Q), then applying DeMorgan and quantifier negation laws to reach an equivalent positive statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation practice: representing everyday mathematical/english statements symbolically
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance and numerous examples show how to represent sentences like 'x is a multiple of y', 'every positive real has a negative square root', or 'everyone likes someone' in quantifier/predicate notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow stepwise construction: identify predicates/constants, choose variable binding and order, add inequalities for uniqueness or non-equality when needed. Examples provided for natural/reals and set-theoretic statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed families and meaning of {x_i | i∈I}
rubrics_metrics.description: An indexed family {x_i | i∈I} denotes the collection of elements x_i indexed by i in I; membership x∈{x_i | i∈I} can be expressed as ∃i∈I(x=x_i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indices need not be numbers (e.g., mothers indexed by students). Equivalent form using elementhood test: {x_i | i∈I} = {x | ∃i∈I(x=x_i)}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of power set and its logical expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: P(A) (power set) is defined as {x | x⊆A}; membership x∈P(A) means ∀y(y∈x → y∈A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: list subsets of a small set, note P(∅) = {∅}. Use this definition when translating statements about power sets into quantified formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union and intersection of a family of sets (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a family F of sets: ⋂F = {x | ∀A∈F (x∈A)} and ⋃F = {x | ∃A∈F (x∈A)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute NF and UF by checking membership in every set vs membership in at least one set. Note: some authors treat ⋂F as undefined when F=∅; caution is advised. Examples illustrate computing ⋂ and ⋃ for concrete families.
